summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Pegasus Retail through JSON mode, typed response schemas, and runtime guardrails; demoed Console runbook for tool autonomy and fallback orchestration. Customer is interested in a 6-week pilot on private VPC with strict latency and audit requirements. Security, KMS, and SSO were flagged as gating items.
topics: Function/tool calling patterns and typed signatures
transcript:
00:00 Sofia Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Sofia from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account, with Ethan our solutions engineer and Maya from product. Can you all hear me okay?
00:08 Rajiv Menon: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks. Diego and Laura here.
00:12 Sofia Park: Awesome. Quick agenda — we'll do a short walkthrough of JSON mode and typed outputs, then show how tool calling and fallback orchestration works end-to-end in the Console, then propose a pilot runbook.
00:25 Ethan Cole: Just a heads up, i'll be jumping into the Console and the API keys briefly. If anyone's sensitive about screenshots, flag it.
00:32 Diego Alvarez: Fine. We're more focused on whether this fits into our private VPC and what the SSO/KMS story looks like.
00:39 Maya Lin: I'll demo how schema tests and a simulate mode live in Console. There are also Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization that can cut cost.
00:47 Rajiv Menon: For context, our use case is product copy generation + automated product tagging that hits downstream inventory tools. We need typed JSON, always, because the downstream is strict.
00:58 Ethan Cole: Perfect. That's exactly what JSON mode is built for — strongly typed responses. We'll show a schema that enforces fields like sku_id, title, category_path, confidence_score (float), and actions array for tool-calls.
01:10 Laura Kim: Quick question: what's the behavior when model outputs don't conform? Do you fall back or sanitize?
01:16 Ethan Cole: Good question. Two layers — first the runtime validates against the schema and will attempt a deterministic repair pass for minor mismatches; second, you can define fallback policies: retry with a stricter temperature, route to a cheaper model, or invoke a safety tool. We demo the fallback orchestration in the runbook.
01:36 Sofia Park: I'll hand over to Ethan for the Console demo.
01:39 Ethan Cole: (screen) Okay, Console — Project Pegasus demo. Here is the schema editor, we add required fields: sku_id (string), price_cents (int), tags (array[string]), should_create_listing (boolean). Notice we can attach function signatures to the actions array, e.g., call_create_listing(payload) with typed attrs.
02:05 Ethan Cole: I'm going to demo a simulated run where the model tries to return free-text; watch the validator kick in.
02:12 System: (console) Ran schema test — 1 failure: price_cents returned as "19.99" (string) expected integer.
02:20 Rajiv Menon: That's great. Does the validator log the raw model output and the repair? We need auditability.
02:27 Ethan Cole: Yes — both raw and canonicalized responses are stored. You get diffs in the trace view and every token cost is recorded. We also push audit logs to your KMS-wrapped storage in Private deployments.
02:40 Diego Alvarez: When you say Private — we really mean VPC and our HSM. Is that supported?
02:45 Sofia Park: Yes. Private deployment supports customer VPC, HSM/KMS integration and on-prem options. We'll share the KMS integration guide after the call.
02:54 Rajiv Menon: Now let's see tool calling. Our pipeline needs the model to call an enrichment API to fetch taxonomy id before writing.
03:02 Ethan Cole: Right — in JSON mode you can define an actions array with typed tool signatures. When the model emits an action, Redwood runtime will call the registered service. If the tool fails, the fallback runbook can either retry, call a secondary tool, or mark the ticket for human review.
03:20 Laura Kim: Can we control which model variant gets used for which route? We might want a cheaper quantized model for tags but a stronger model for copy.
03:27 Maya Lin: Absolutely — routing policies allow model-by-route selection, you can set SLOs and cost budgets, and Optimize will recommend quantization profiles per workload.
03:36 Ethan Cole: I'm going to trigger a live call — model returns an actions array with invoke_enrich_tool: {taxonomy_query: "women summer dresses"} and then we see the tool call with a 120ms latency.
03:50 System: (console/trace) Tool call invoke_enrich_tool payload posted to http://internal-enrichsvc/resolve -> 200 OK, response: {taxonomy_id: "TAX-1234"}
04:02 Rajiv Menon: Latency looks ok. How does KV cache play with tool calls? If the same SKU is looked up repeatedly we want to avoid calls.
04:10 Ethan Cole: There's prefix KV caching for embeddings and a response caching layer for tool responses. Note that KV cache semantics are pluggable — you can set TTLs per keyspace.
04:20 Diego Alvarez: Small nit — we get a lot of misspell in docs; you said KV cash. (laughs)
04:24 Ethan Cole: (laughs) yeah, my bad, K-V cache.
04:28 Rajiv Menon: Show us a failure mode where schema repair can't fix it and falls through to human.
04:33 Ethan Cole: Sure — I'll simulate a schema mismatch where actions is a string not an array. Console shows the failed validation, then our runbook routes to a human review queue and creates a ticket.
04:50 System: (console) Validation failed: actions expected array, got string. Runbook: open manual review -> Slack alert -> create ticket in JIRA (project PEGASUS-ML).
05:02 Laura Kim: Ok, audit trail is important. Do you retain the raw model tokens? Regulatory wants six month retention, and we need to redact PII.
05:11 Sofia Park: Retention windows are configurable; we support automatic redaction rules and we can integrate with your DLP to mask PII before logs leave your VPC.
05:21 Rajiv Menon: On security, can users authenticate via SSO and get role-based access to runbooks?
05:27 Maya Lin: Yes — SSO (SAML/SCIM) + RBAC is supported. We can map roles to Console capabilities, and all API keys rotate automatically.
05:33 Diego Alvarez: Show me the Optimize tab, how do batching suggestions look?
05:37 Ethan Cole: Optimize pulls your token distribution, seq lengths, and recommends batch sizes and a quantization profile. For example the recommendation here suggests dynamic batching up to 8 for short tag requests, plus a q4_0 quant profile for less-critical routes that reduce cost ~45%.
05:57 Rajiv Menon: Are those recommendations safe to auto-apply? We can't break quality.
06:02 Maya Lin: They are suggestions — you can preview estimated latency/cost impact and run a canary. We also tie evaluation metrics back to prompt suites so you can detect regressions before rolling out.
06:15 Sofia Park: Quick demo of simulate mode — you can force the model to return a specific error to see runbook behavior without real traffic.
06:22 Ethan Cole: (simulate) Forcing tool failure: runbook retries 2x then routes to fallback model which returns a degraded but schema-valid response, then human review.
06:34 Rajiv Menon: That's handy. How do you ensure deterministic repairs? Sometimes we need the exact raw output for audit.
06:41 Ethan Cole: We keep raw outputs unmodified in an append-only log. Repairs are new artifacts layered on top — all diffs are visible. You control whether downstream gets canonicalized or raw.
06:52 Diego Alvarez: Let's talk pilot. We want to scope a 6-week pilot: private VPC, 50k calls/day, latency p99 under 350ms for tagging, and automated audits. Will Redwood support that?
07:06 Sofia Park: Yes, typical Dedicated/Private pilots look like that. We'll propose a runbook: week 0 onboarding and network setup, week 1 schema onboarding and console training, week 2 small traffic run, weeks 3–4 canary + quality evals, week 5 scale tests, week 6 handoff.
07:23 Rajiv Menon: Cost question — how do you price Private? We need a predictable model.
07:28 Sofia Park: Pricing for Private is a platform fee plus usage; for pilots we often do a short-term committed quota to make costs predictable. We'll share a ballpark.
07:35 Laura Kim: Any blockers on our side besides SSO and KMS? We have strict IP allowlists and will need peering.
07:42 Ethan Cole: We'll need a networking contact for peering and to validate our private endpoints. Also a brief security call for KMS key wrapping details.
07:51 Rajiv Menon: Competitors question — how is this different from Anthropic or OpenAI endpoints?
07:56 Maya Lin: Two main differences — one, unified runtime with typed schema enforcement and tool orchestration built-in; two, production controls like route-level model routing, prefix caching, and built-in runbooks for fallback. Others provide model endpoints but fewer ops primitives.
08:12 Diego Alvarez: Any examples of real customers with similar flows?
08:16 Sofia Park: We have a retail customer case study doing catalog enrichment with JSON mode; happy to share the anonymized deck.
08:21 Rajiv Menon: Can you show an example schema for our catalog?
08:24 Ethan Cole: (pasting) Example: {"required":["sku_id","title","tags"], "properties": {"sku_id":{"type":"string"}, "price_cents":{"type":"integer"}, "tags":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}, "actions":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"object","properties":{"name":{"type":"string"},"args":{"type":"object"}}}}}}
08:47 Rajiv Menon: That looks good. When you attach a function signature, can it surface in the SDK so engineers don't hand-roll parsing?
08:55 Ethan Cole: Yes — function signatures are exported in SDK types (TypeScript/Python) so you get typed client calls and auto-serialized payloads.
09:05 Laura Kim: About backups and logs — do you let us push audit logs to our S3 behind our KMS?
09:11 Sofia Park: Yes, in Private we can deliver logs to your S3 and they stay encrypted with your key.
09:16 Rajiv Menon: Let's fast-forward — sample failure: model hallucinated a category_id. Show how you detect and revert.
09:22 Ethan Cole: (simulate) Model returned category_id "9999". Our quality checks run a rerank check against a cached taxonomy and flag low-confidence items for human review; we also have an automatic fallback to a deterministic rule-based enricher.
09:40 Diego Alvarez: One operational ask: can runbook steps be conditional on metadata like tenant or model_variant?
09:45 Maya Lin: Yes, runbooks support conditional branching and matchers on request metadata — you can route by customer, route, or latency.
09:53 Rajiv Menon: Ok — let's capture the risks: 1) latency during peaks, 2) schema drift, 3) audit retention — we need mitigations.
10:05 Sofia Park: Mitigations: autoscaling policies + burst pools for latency, schema monitor with regression alerts for drift, and configurable retention + redaction for audit. We'll put all of that in the pilot runbook.
10:18 Laura Kim: Anything around data residency for EU? We have EU catalog data.
10:22 Sofia Park: We have region controls; we can pin traffic and storage to EU regions for residency.
10:27 Rajiv Menon: Great. A couple of quick clarifications before we wrap — what's the estimated timeline to get a private pilot up if we say yes next week?
10:34 Sofia Park: Usually 2–3 weeks to stand up networking and access, then the 6-week pilot cadence. So full 8–9 weeks to completion from kick-off.
10:43 Diego Alvarez: Ok. Who's responsible for PKI and peering? We'll loop in infra.
10:48 Sofia Park: We'll share a network checklist and point of contact.
10:52 Rajiv Menon: End of my list. Any outstanding items from Redwood?
10:56 Ethan Cole: We'll send the schema templates and console export, plus a proposed pilot SOW.
11:01 Sofia Park: I'll share SOC2/KMS docs and pricing. Also adding a short 30-min engineering deep-dive to run the VPC test.
11:08 Rajiv Menon: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
11:11 Sofia Park: Thanks all — we'll follow up with materials.
11:15 System: Meeting ended. Record length 62:03.
